newsitem.title: UK: No easy ride for Eurotunnel deal - bankers.
newsitem.headline: No easy ride for Eurotunnel deal - bankers.

text.p: LONDON, Oct 3, Reuter - A bankers' meeting to review a restructuring deal on nine billion pounds ($14 billion) of debt owed by channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA/Plc is unlikely to be a mere formality, bankers said on Thursday.
The London meeting on Friday brings together the six members of the debt steering committee and a group of 26 instructing banks who in turn represent the 225 lenders to Eurotunnel.
Bankers warned that the meeting would be no rubber-stamp operation and that all the banks had to be convinced about the deal for it to fly.

"Because of the structure of the deal, all it takes is for one bank to reject it and the whole thing could be in difficulties," one banking source said. "Everything is very optimistic but there has to be a chance of failure."
The fact that there are 225 lenders means the process will be a delicate one.
Details are scant of of the deal, thrashed out over the last year and agreed in dramatic style earlier this week.
But an expected debt-for-equity swap giving the banks an immediate 49 pct of Eurotunnel equity in return for the retiring of some 1.5 billion pounds of debt seems to be a central plank.
The other is a large convertible bond-for-debt swap which could take out a further 2.0 to 2.5 billion pounds of the firm's obligations and potentially gives the banks control over it.
The two sides are also thought to have agreed an instrument to take care of unpaid interest accrued since Eurotunnel froze interest payments on its debt in September 1995.
Banking sources say Eurotunnel's lenders are likely to come under intense pressure to accept the deal since the alternative, a further move towards insolvency, is unlikely to be good news for anyone.
"That's why a deal was done," said one banker. "There comes a point when the posturing has to stop and the alternatives considered."
Bankers say respective central banks are also likely to be involved, especially as both the French and British governments have some political capital at stake in the Eurotunnel project.

"Our experience of these matters is that the Bank (of England) is very likely to take a look at the deal and urge agreement," another banking source, who declined to be named, said. "Let's just put it that way."
Bankers are not only worried that a disagreement among themselves could scupper the deal.
They say Japanese banks, owed around a quarter of the total debt, could have problems because of the unfavourable tax treatment which could follow a debt-for-equity deal.
In previous cases, Japanese banks have been able to sell their portion of the debt in the secondary market, thus realising their loss and writing it off against tax.
But, in the case of Eurotunnel, the amounts are too big and the Japanese banks, unless another solution can be found, will have to carry the loans on their books.
Bankers are also concerned that Eurotunnel shareholders could be unhappy that the convertible bond element of the deal gives potential control of the company to the lenders if they convert the paper.
But, as with the other elements, the theory is they will realise that a bit of something viable is better than nothing.
"It may be a bit of a struggle. Someone tends to make a fuss at some point, but, all in all, I expect the deal to go through," one banker said. ($1=.6388 Pound)
